defs_parts: Seven labels sit in the corners of the pictures that follow.
In the book text: the course text uses and explains the term.
In the glossary: the term is on the course term list, but the text does not explain it.
Video only: the term comes from a video lecture, and is not in the course text or on the term list.
Computed: the numbers are worked out on screen from stated inputs.
Simulation: a model run step by step from stated rules, not a measurement of a real game.
Illustrative data: numbers chosen to show the idea, not measured.
Conceptual: a drawing of the idea, with no data behind it.
recap_lines: Clarity is telling what is going on, and satisfaction is feeling good to act.
Contrast is one difference, and visual hierarchy is the order the eye visits.
A silhouette must still say what it is, filled black at game size.
Concept art solves a design problem, and its polish hardly matters.
Constraints narrow the ideas, and closing doors drops the weaker ones each round.
A high-poly sculpt's detail is baked onto the low-poly mesh the engine runs.
bookends.segment: Name The Art Term, Defend It
bookends.command: Quiz me on game art terms with short game-making cases, one at a time. Use the terms clarity, satisfaction, visual hierarchy, contrast, silhouette, readability, reference, mood board, proxy model and low-poly mesh. For each case I must name the exact term and say why its look-alike is wrong. Hold back the answer until I reply, then tell me if I was right.
checks: Check: each case is a game-making situation, and the answer waits for you.
Check: you named the exact term and said why its look-alike is wrong.
